text_to_read: Lesson 1: What is a matrix?
A matrix is a set of boxes arranged in straight lines, like the benches in a classroom.
Each box is called a cell.
A row goes from left to right. A column goes straight forward, away from you.
Row 1 is the row nearest to you. When you move forward, the row number grows: row 1, row 2, row 3. Column 1 is on your left. When you move right, the column number grows.
We write the size of a matrix as m × n. We read it as m by n. m is the number of rows, and n is the number of columns.
A 3 × 4 matrix has 3 rows and 4 columns. So it has 3 times 4, that is 12 cells.
Now practise. Press Tab to go to the matrix. It is a 3 × 3 matrix, and every cell tells you its row and column. Move around with the arrow keys. When you are ready for the exercises, press Alt N.

Lesson 2: The address of a cell
Every cell has an address. We write it as (row, column).
(2, 3) means row 2, column 3. The row always comes first, then the column.
In these exercises, only the first cell, (1, 1), tells you its address. Every other cell makes a dot sound, so count your steps. If you bump into the edge, you will hear a thud.
You always start at (1, 1). When you think you are on the right cell, press Enter. Press R to hear the question again. Press Alt N to begin.

Lesson 6: Corners, edges and the middle
Some places in a matrix are easy to find without counting. We call them landmarks.
A corner has walls on two sides. In a corner, you hear a thud in two directions. There are four corners: near-left, near-right, far-left and far-right.
Near means row 1, the row closest to you. Far means the last row. An edge is the whole line of cells next to a wall.
The middle cell has the same number of steps to the walls on each side. In a 5 by 5 matrix, the middle is row 3, column 3.
Only the start cell, (1, 1), speaks. Go to the place and press Enter. Press Alt N to begin.

Lesson 7: How far?
How far apart are two cells? Count the steps along the column and the steps along the row, then add them.
From (2, 1) to (4, 4): the row changes from 2 to 4, that is 2 steps. The column changes from 1 to 4, that is 3 steps. 2 plus 3 is 5 steps.

Lesson 10: Diagonal steps
Until now you moved forward, back, left or right. Now you can also move on a slant: diagonally.
One diagonal step changes the row and the column together. Forward-right adds one to the row and one to the column: from (1, 1) you go to (2, 2).
The keys: E or Page Up is forward-right. Q or Home is forward-left. C or Page Down is back-right. Z or End is back-left. On a number pad, use 9, 7, 3 and 1.
If a diagonal step would go past a wall, you hear the thud and stay where you are.

text_to_read: Lesson 11: The main diagonal
The main diagonal is the slanted line of cells from the near-left corner to the far-right corner: (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), and so on.
On the main diagonal, the row number and the column number are the same.
To walk along it, start at (1, 1) and press forward-right again and again, until you hear the thud.
If the matrix is not square, the diagonal stops at the first wall it reaches. Press Alt N to begin.

There is a second diagonal. It goes from the near-right corner to the far-left corner. In a 5 by 5 matrix: (1, 5), (2, 4), (3, 3), (4, 2), (5, 1).
On this diagonal, row plus column is always the same. In a 5 by 5 matrix it is 6: 1 plus 5, 2 plus 4, and so on.

Now the cells hold numbers. In an identity matrix, every cell on the main diagonal holds 1, and every other cell holds 0.
It is a square matrix: it has as many rows as columns. It is used a lot in mathematics, and you will meet it again later.

Lesson 18: Turn the matrix
Turning a matrix makes its rows into columns. Row 1 becomes column 1, row 2 becomes column 2, and so on. In mathematics this is called the transpose.
So the thing at (2, 3) moves to (3, 2): the row number and the column number swap places.
A 2 by 3 matrix becomes a 3 by 2 matrix. The cells on the main diagonal, like (1, 1) and (2, 2), stay where they are. Press Alt N to begin.
